Editorial

Monica Lanyado and Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards  

This edition of the journal continues to reflect the increasingly international nature of our readers and contributors. It is fascinating to hear about work in Denmark (Liselotte Grunbaum), Italy (Gabriella Pansini) and Greece (Dimitris Anastasopoulos) that resonates so clearly with work going on elsewhere. Four papers (by Meira Likierman, Lynda Miller, Dimitris Anastasopoulos and Peter Evans) discuss adolescent processes — a fact that belies the journal's title, a title which does not, in fact, fully reflect our interests, which include not only adolescence, but also very young children and babies.

We are also very pleased to include three papers given by the authors at major international conferences — two in London (Penelope Leach and Meira Likierman) and one in Athens (Liselotte Grunbaum). At times there can be a sense of exponential growth in the number of interesting conferences and papers being given in our profession, leading to a sense that it is impossible to keep up with all the stimulating ideas that are buzzing around. The recent EFPP (European Federation of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, Child Section) conference in Stockholm was a prime example of the amount of high-quality, interesting work going on throughout Europe. Publishing papers that have been given at conferences helps to spread these ideas. So we would like to encourage more of our readers to send us conference papers and lectures they have given, so that their hard work in preparing these papers reaches as large an audience as possible.

We are privileged to open this edition of the journal with the lecture given by Penelope Leach as the Anna Freud Centenary Lecture in London in November 1995: ‘Attachment: facing the professional demands of today's research findings’. Her work is possibly best known through her many publications on child care and development for the general public, about which she feels passionately and in which she has had considerable influence. This stimulating lecture provided the opportunity to hear her talking from an academic perspective about her views on research findings on attachment, separation and loss.

The Structure of Internal Space: Conditions for Change in a 6-Year-Old Girl with Severe Developmental Delay

Gabriella Pansini

Gabriella Pansini

Via Vespucci 4
Turin
Italy

Gabriella Pansini  

Internal world; two-dimensional space; mental concreteness; verbal and non-verbal communication.

From the analysis of a developmentally delayed 6-year-old girl, with possible organic complications and with some mild autistic features, the author shows how the internal organization of space is related to the perception of relations with real external objects and between these objects. Conversely, the internal configuration of space and object relations influences the way the outside world is known and experienced. The inner world of this little girl was characterized by the complete concreteness of her ideas, and by a two-dimensional conception of space, used to defend against intrusion by persecutory figures. In the therapeutic relationship this was the cause of enormous difficulties both for verbal communication and for initiating change. The author explains how, through the expression of her own countertransference to the child, communication was established and lasting change achieved.

Julia Fabricius

Julia Fabricius

The Anna Freud Centre

Julia Fabricius  

The title of this book refers to the ubiquitous clinical phenomenon whereby an individual, by the use of a mental mechanism which the Novick's call ‘externalization’, strives in every way to bring about a relationship in which devalued aspects of the self can be attributed to, and elicited in, the object. The Novick's show, in careful detail, how this defence is used both to avoid narcissistic pain and to deny the object's separate existence, that is, as a means of maintaining the phantasy of an omnipotent self. They also demonstrate the serious pathological effects of an extreme or persistent use of this defence at any period of life, including the effects on children of its use by parents, delineate the course of its development from infancy onwards and discuss the technical implications of their findings. A brief anecdote illustrates the way their title strikes a chord of familiarity. By some error I was sent two copies of the book, which I placed side by side on a high shelf in my book case. The next day, in a session well into the analysis of a patient with whose treatment I have received considerable help from my earlier reading of the Novicks’ papers, I made an interpretation about how much she wished that I should experience her feelings in exactly the same helpless way that she did. She did not reply directly but scanned the bookcase, focused on the remote top shelf and asked: ‘Why do you have two copies of Fearful Symmetry?

The Novicks are child and adult psychoanalysts working in Michigan who received analytic training in England and worked for some years at the Hampstead clinic (now Anna Freud Centre) before returning to the US. The book contains both previously published papers (not necessarily in chronological order)

Anastasia Widdicombe

Anastasia Widdicombe

75 Albert Street
London NW1 7LX

Anastasia Widdicombe  

‘The theories of Philosophers are necessarily concealed autobiography’ (Nietzsche). Winnicott's theories are variously received as uniquely illuminating or as opaque and difficult. Brett Kahr now gives us a glimpse of the biography behind the work and ideas of the world-renowned paediatrician and psychoanalyst. Although it is the first whole book devoted to Winnicott's life it remains a sketch rather than a comprehensive biography and will be followed by a more extended piece of biographical research and a guide to Winnicott's published work by the same author.

There are perils in writing the biography of someone who is still remembered, and still controversial. In an introduction to the Biographical Portrait, Dr Susanna Isaacs Elmhirst, a psychoanalyst who had a long involvement with Winnicott and his work with children and parents in the NHS, cautions readers to approach Kahr's sketch (and indeed their thoughts about Winnicott) with a healthily sceptical appetite but concedes that in this book Kahr does ‘strike home’ a great deal. Although Kahr does not attempt to review Winnicott's work or to trace the influence of his ideas within the development of psychoanalysis he does engage with some of the contradictions in the life of this subtle and interesting man and in how his work was received. He was the first man to qualify in child psychoanalysis, was chosen by Melanie Klein to analyse one of her own children and was twice President of the British Psycho-Analytical Society.

Editorial

Monica Lanyado and Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards  

It is five years since there was last an edition of the journal which focused on work with babies and children under 5 (Vol. 18, No. 2). Since that time there has been an enormous increase in Britain and around the world in work with parents and children in the earliest years. It is important and timely to reflect on this growth and to publish papers which keep us up to date with clinical and theoretical developments, thus informing our practice and giving us the opportunity to generate interest beyond the profession in early intervention.

We open this edition with Dilys Daws’ paper ‘The perils of intimacy: closeness and distance in feeding and weaning’ in which the author, who works in London, discusses early feeding difficulties with reference to the process of weaning as well as the unmet needs of the parents. She draws on baby observation material to illustrate her interesting ideas about the difficulties that parents can have in establishing the appropriate emotional distance between themselves and their baby and discusses the use of the spoon as a transitional object within this process.

In ‘The little alien: links between mind and body in parent-infant psychotherapy’, Maria Theresa Gallo from Italy documents the remarkable progress which was made by an 18-month-old baby originally diagnosed as autistic, when she saw him together with his mother. His pathological defences receded dramatically as Dr Gallo modified ‘classical’ psychoanalytic technique while working within a firmly psychodynamic framework. This enabled this child to travel from ‘outer space’ into relationship with his mother and those around him.

In the past two years we have been fortunate to be able to publish work done in Australia with the parents of premature babies (Vol. 21, No. 1 and Vol. 22, No. 2). In this edition Frances Thomson-Salo and Campbell Paul, who work in Melbourne, Australia, write about ‘Infant-led innovations in a mother-baby therapy group’.

Maria Gallo  

Joint psychotherapy; individual psychotherapy; autism; development; relationship; separation.

This paper presents psychotherapy with a mother-child couple in which the little boy was originally diagnosed as autistic. The case was based on psychoanalytic understanding, but symbolic interpretations to analyse unconscious dynamics activated in the transference were not used, because the child was not able to use his mind to ‘think’ in ways appropriate to his age. The technique was adapted to circumstances that included the reduced comprehension of the child, his pressing developmental needs and the narcissistic personality of the mother, together with her lack of empathy. Interpretations were directed to both of them, in order to promote, simultaneously, the child's development and the couple's capacity to relate to each other. The child progressed rapidly and the symptomatology receded. With hindsight, the presenting autistic symptoms can be ascribed to the early onset of pathological defences as a consequence of illness and separation during the first week of life.

The Little Obsessional Alchemist

Joan Symington

Joan Symington

PO Box 87, Pymble 2073
Sydney, NSW
Australia

Joan Symington  

Psychoanalytic insight; selected fact; obsessionality; alchemy; psychoanalytic theory; pseudo-reparation; incoherence; precipitation of coherence.

Using the psychoanalytic experience with an obsessional child, this paper looks at the moment of insight, that precipitation of coherence which occurs when we say that we suddenly realize something. This is contrasted with the approach of consciously trying to fit theory to the observed facts. Analogies with alchemy are drawn. In addition, the balancing process occurring in obsessional mentality is compared with strangulation by hanging, the opposing forces being comprised of prematurely solidified states of mind such as mania or paranoia which interfere with that fluid state of mind optimal for the precipitation of insight.

This book aims to highlight the variety of ways in which psychoanalytic ideas and psychodynamic methods can be utilized and adapted in diverse community settings. It is primarily aimed at professionals of all disciplines who work with children and families who are troubled with emotional and behavioural problems.

The book is divided into five sections covering an introduction to key analytic concepts, individuals and families, groups, organizations and social issues. An interesting device is the use of a ‘link’ chapter between the sections which outlines the key analytic concepts involved in the work and how these are illustrated in each chapter.

Each of the chapters is written by an individual with considerable experience and expertise in a spectrum of work in community settings.

Geoffrey Baruch  

This monograph is a compilation of papers written by members of staff of Brent Adolescent Centre (formerly Brent Consultation Centre) on the suicidal adolescent and the proceedings of a conference held in 1993 devoted to this topic. I must confess that having worked at the Centre for a number of years it is difficult to provide a dispassionate review when much of what I have learned about working with troubled adolescents, including suicidal adolescents, was at the ‘knees’ of Moses and Egle Laufer. However, I hope I am able to suspend this closeness to the authors for the sake of the review.

The book is timely. The increase of psychosocial disorders in young people has recently been documented in an authoritative volume of research findings edited by Rutter and Smith (1995). Diekstra, Kienhorst and de Wilde (1995) show that the rate of suicide and attempted suicide in young people increased between the early 1950s and the early 1980s, that in the last decade suicide rates in young men have continued to rise and those in young women have remained stable. The rates for attempted suicide have fallen, although there is a debate about whether the observed decline in attempted suicide is an artefact due to the underreporting of attempted suicide to medical agencies. Certainly my own clinical experience and that of the Brent Adolescent Centre and other similar agencies would suggest that there has been anything but a decline in attempted suicide and deliberate self-harm.

The Suicidal Adolescent is devoted to the clinical issues concerned with adolescents who present with suicidal behaviour seen from a psychoanalytic perspective. The book is divided into two parts.

Correspondence

Anne Alverez

Anne Alverez

120 Belsize Lane
London NW3 5BA

Anne Alverez  

Letter to the Editors from Mrs Anne Alvarez, Child and Family Department, Tavistock Clinic, London

I wanted to make only one or two comments on Gabriella Pansini's rich and fascinating paper, ‘The Structure of Internal Space: conditions for change in a six-year-old girl with severe developmental delay’, Journal of Child Psychotherapy, 23(1), 25-49. The concept of the structural deficit in Benedetta's notion of three-dimensional space is beautifully explored by Pansini herself, so I simply wish to underline the idea that the baby could not sit up and reach out to life nor the child listen with interest to the words of others, until her object was sufficiently valuable, interesting, quiet and powerfully human to attract her interest. Betty Joseph has been writing for years, and John Steiner more recently, about the need to contain, without prematurely returning, the projective identifications of borderline patients. But, Pansini's moving example goes further: it is interesting that the child saw her therapist's wordless sorrow first, and only then did she ask for, and listen to, an explanation. It is also interning that the therapist did not say ‘you feel that I am worried’. She said ‘Because I am worried about you’. This raises the important issue of when and whether a ‘you’ interpretation can overload and overwhelm a patient who is confused about I-you differentiations, has little self-reflective capacity, and little sense of self. Often I think we overwhelm a patient at such moments when we locate the feeling too firmly in them. Harold Sears and Bryce Boyer, both experts in work with adult psychotics, have used a similar method of owning countertransferences fully. It may not seem like psychoanalysis, but does that matter if it works? Or should we stretch our definitions of psychoanalysis when we work with patients who cannot think?

Yours sincerely

Editorial

Monica Lanyado and Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards  

This December 1997 edition of the journal bears witness, with the addition of a subtitle to our name, to the increasingly international spread of our work. The subtitle, ‘International clinical and theoretical contributions on work with infants, children, adolescents and their families’, reflects not only the growing international profile of our profession, but also better describes the scope of the work we do. In addition, this particular issue also demonstrates the increasing focus we need to maintain on how political and social developments around the world impact on the work. This is addressed here through a sub-section on trauma, and the edition also includes research into turning points, preventive work and the potentiating factors which pave the way to healthier functioning.

In ‘Laughter opens the door’, Gunnar Carlberg from Stockholm examines the fascinating subject of turning points in treatment. His research involved work with five child psychotherapists, who were interviewed just after a session with a child where they noticed something qualitatively new in terms of the child's expression of internal world dynamics. Follow-up interviews with the therapists, their own supervision and parallel work with parents are described. This paper researches something which lies at the heart of our work, and is an important contribution to our understanding.

Giuliana De Astis from Rome describes work with young autistic/psychotic children which includes an interesting way of working with parents that has been established for a number of years in Rome. Her paper, ‘Thoughts about the development of a potential space in the psychoanalytic treatment of infantile psychosis’, draws on Winnicott's concept of the growth of ‘potential space’ in therapy as part of the recovery process. She illustrates her thesis with three cases, one of which includes a complete session of joint mother-child work, highlighting the difficulties of creating this potential space.

Meira Likierman

Meira Likierman

5 Downshire Hill

Meira Likierman  

Anorexia; adolescent; feminine; maternal; intrusive; containment; baby; ugly; fat.

In this paper I put forward a hypothesis on a particular psycho-sexual determinant of anorexia nervosa in adolescent girls. I begin with an overview of existing literature which examines anorexia from psychiatric, demographic, medical, historical and psychoanalytic viewpoints. Drawing on the theories of Freud, Klein, Winnicott and Bion, and building on previous thinking, I posit a specific disturbance in the psychic development of the adolescent girl. I suggest that this amounts to her rebellion against the psychic onset of her future maternal capacities for reverie and containment. I link this disturbance to a pathological mother-daughter relationship and illustrate my hypothesis with a clinical account of intensive, long-term work with an adolescent girl. The high motivation and vivid dream material of this patient make for a particularly rewarding study.

Susan Budd  

This is a good and important book. It is also very interesting on what might be called the level of the higher gossip. It could well have been subtitled, ‘Or What Psychoanalysts Really Think’.

Before she became a child psychotherapist and an analyst, Victoria Hamilton was trained as a philosopher, sophisticated in the notions of language games and questions of mutual intelligibility between different traditions of thought. Knowing that psychoanalysis is not a discipline — maybe there are no such disciplines — in which knowledge has been systematically amassed within a coherent framework, she set out to look at how analysts belonging to several different theoretical schools used their ideas in practice.

She interviewed sixty-five psychoanalysts in New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles (where she now works) and London, between 1988 and 1990. She surveyed the literature on analytic technique, and asked analysts to describe their use of different technical concepts which were drawn from twenty-seven dimensions of technique. This produced ‘various descriptions of the maps or sketches analysts drew of the routes they followed in their daily practice’. Then, by means of cluster analysis, she was able to establish the relationship between their beliefs, the extent to which subgroups of analysts held homogeneous or eclectic views both as individuals and as groups, and the difference between ‘official’ beliefs and what analysts said that they actually did. The bulk of the book is made up of long excerpts from the transcripts of what the analysts told her — often indicating how their views had changed, and how what they had been taught, or felt they were supposed to believe, no longer seemed to fit their clinical experience.

Tim Dartington  

It is unfortunately rare that the insights of social science in general and psychology in particular are applied in a purposeful way to issues of

455

public policy. So this book of essays by British social scientists, clinicians and politicians is unusual as well as timely. Why is the application of psychological insights to political debate so inhibited? A reluctance of clinicians to expose their public face? There have been applications of attachment theory through action research projects, for example Isabel Menzies Lyth and colleagues at the Tavistock Institute following up the work of James and Joyce Robertson with a study of daycare for the under-5s. (I was involved with her also in work on the psychological needs of small children in hospital.) In his chapter on ‘Attachment in context’, Michael Rustin makes reference to this and other work. He also links attachment to the theories of containment associated with Bion, and much used by clinicians and psychoanalytically informed organizational consultants in recent times.

In general, however, psychoanalysts have spoken out on nuclear war more freely than on the dilemmas of a divided society. It is not certain even now that the world is ready for a public policy that is truly informed by psychological insights. In this book, Tessa Jowell, MP, makes reference to the scorn that Antidote, an organization founded by psychotherapists to promote ‘emotional literacy’ in politics, got even in the pages of the liberal-minded Guardian newspaper. She and Marjorie Mowlam, another Labour MP, both speak about the insecurities of politicians, which have to be denied, and the insecurities of the citizen, which have to be faced.

This book, inspired by a conference at the Tavistock Clinic in London, explores the applications of attachment theory to a wide range of policy issues. John Bowlby was foremost among psychoanalysts as a pioneer of empirical research. His ideas have been buffeted by political fashion. He was not forgiven for the starkness of his original propositions — e.g. that separation from the mother leads to delinquency — challenged with equal vigour by Michael Rutter. In the 1970s his ideas were resented as patrician and hostile to the women's movement. It was a time when women as well as children were leaving home. There is now an upsurge in concern about social cohesion — and the sub-title of this book is ‘Towards a Stable Society’.

Nicholas Wall cheerfully quips in his introduction to this collection of papers of the 1995 Dartington Hall Conference: ‘I have often heard it said that conference papers are the kiss of death to publishers.’ I am happy to report that this expectation is unfounded and that this publication is well worth the reading. To bring together some twenty-eight judges and a roughly equal number of psychoanalytically trained child professionals and invite them to exchange papers to encourage discussion was a welcome idea.

I approached the book with a sense of intrigue as to how that inaccessible world of the courtroom and the law would view child psychotherapists. What sense do judges make of us as ‘expert witnesses’ trying to convey our sense of a child's faltering account of their abuse or their hopes and fears about living at home? What would judges want us to address in our court reports. Can they appreciate a therapist's qualms on a client's right to confidentiality.

Janine Sternberg

Janine Sternberg

Tavistock Mulberry Bush Day Unit
33 Daleham Gardens
London NW3

Janine Sternberg  

I am writing with some thoughts and questions following Campbell Paul and Frances Thomson-Salo's most interesting paper about ‘infantled

468

innovations in a mother-baby therapy group’. I was fortunate to see excerpts of their video material and hear them speak about their ideas at an ACP Scientific Meeting in London last summer. I think that without that experience (of seeing some evidence of the infants’ interest in and responsiveness to each other), it might have been more difficult to go along with the ideas expressed about the therapeutic value of infant to infant interaction. Even so, the paper still left me with many unanswered questions.

Many professionals offer post-natal support groups for women, and both the need for them and the value of them are widely recognized. It is often not possible to have a male co-worker, but the comments about the particular role Campbell Paul played certainly highlight how useful a ‘father figure’ can be. The major difference between Campbell Paul and Frances Thomson-Salo's group work as described, and others I have come across, lies in the emphasis that they place on the infants as equal group members. This, perhaps due to its unfamiliarity, is the most questionable part, with many of us I am sure, wondering about the implications of the statement ‘no child is too young for direct psychotherapeutic work’.

It was most interesting to read the authors’ descriptions of the way in which they interact with the infants, taking care to address them directly and ‘holding the infant's gaze while we think about her and respond to her is, we think, one of our most significant interventions’. They explain how they relate to the infants through attunement, and how they use ‘the language of action and play’, and they acknowledge that they not only followed but also initiated interaction with the child. They describe this as ‘minimal’ in action but powerful in effect and they give a very dramatic example of this. There are surely issues to be discussed here about the difference, if any, between this and the ‘modelling’ for the mothers which they say they avoid doing.

Attachment: Facing the Professional Demands of Today's Research Findings

Penelope Leach

Penelope Leach

3 Tanza Rd
London NW3 2UA

Penelope Leach  

Attachment theory; day care provision; maternal deprivation; history of maternal care; positive attachment.

The author places maternal deprivation, attachment theory and the debate concerning child care by mothers or others, in the sociopolitical and historical context of the latter half of the twentieth century. It is suggested that post-war political pressures, motivated by economic concerns, led to selective over-simplification of complex theory and research findings. This has led to a polarization of views on solutions to the conflict between traditional child care by mothers at home and their modern wage earning outside it, and to assumptions about day care that may not be warranted.

The author briefly describes the results of an opinion survey, supported by Mary Ainsworth. Members of an international organization of infant mental health professionals were asked to give their anonymous views concerning optimal choices among high-quality kinds of care for infants from birth to three and a half years. Results suggest that professional, well-informed opinion is not being effectively communicated to public opinion and policy makers. Finally, the author expresses the hope that current research may finally free attachment theory from the concept of maternal deprivation and the backlash that has so undervalued motherhood.

Pervasive Traumatic Loss from AIDS in the Life of a 4-Year-Old African Boy

Annette Mendelsohn

Annette Mendelsohn

Traumatic Stress Clinic
73 Charlotte Street
London W1P 1LB

Annette Mendelsohn  

AIDS; traumatic bereavement; child survivors.

It is estimated that, by the end of this century, over five million children under the age of 10 will have lost their mothers as a result of HIV infection. The psychological implications for the children who survive are extensive. These children suffer not only from bereavements and disruption to family life, they also suffer from prevailing anxieties about their own health and the health of their carers. It is the pervasive threat of death which constitutes chronic trauma for child survivors of HIV infection. Confusions abound in fact and in phantasy of where responsibility lies for the tragedies which surround them. Psychotherapeutic treatment for the survivors concentrates on both the cognitive and the emotional aspects of the traumas to enable the child to grieve and to feel appropriate anger for the tragedy in their life. This paper presents a detailed case history of a 4-year-old African boy of refugee parents who were victims of war as well as AIDS. Using a psychoanalytic framework, the child's distorted perceptions of his world are described and his attempts to make sense of his world and keep hope alive in spite of the continual threat of abandonment is demonstrated.

Parent-Infant Psychotherapy: A Review Article

Bristol England

Bristol England

Knowle Clinic
Broadfield Road
Bristol BS4 2UH

Bristol England  

The relatively new field of parent-infant psychotherapy, while largely dominated by the paradigms provided by psychoanalysis and attachment theory, also encompasses considerable diversity. Stern's latest book, The Motherhood Constellation, attempts to offer an overview of these different approaches and he accordingly subtitles his work ‘A Unified View of Parent-Infant Psychotherapy’ (Stern, 1995).

According to Stern, and here he is developing a thesis previously adumbrated in an article in the Infant Mental Health Journal (Stern-Bruschweiler and Stern, 1989), all the different therapeutic modalities, competently practised, are equally effective. He accounts for this by arguing that the ‘Clinical System’, as he terms it, is interactive in nature so that a change in one area of the system will necessarily lead to changes in other areas. For example, a change in the mother's representation of the infant (the privileged target of a more psychoanalytic approach) would lead to a change in the mother's behaviour towards the infant and hence a change in the infant's response, but equally a change made to the mother's behaviour towards the infant (as in a more behavioural approach) would lead to a corresponding change in the infant's response and hence to a change in the mother's representation of the infant. In consequence it matters little which ‘port of entry’ into the system is used since the effect will pervade the whole system.

Bertrand Cramer, a colleague of Stern in Geneva, is in no doubt which ‘port of entry’ he prefers and his recent (1993) book on The Practice of Mother-Infant Psychotherapy, co-authored with Francisco Palacio-Espasa, gives a vivid account of his avowedly psychoanalytic approach. It is a book I would warmly recommend to all those interested in this area of work, though regrettably it seems unlikely that it will be translated into English.

Laughter Opens the Door: Turning Points in Child Psychotherapy

Gunnar Carlberg

Gunnar Carlberg

Odengatan 9
S-114 24 Stockholm
Sweden

Gunnar Carlberg  

With the aim of increasing knowledge about processes of change in psychodynamic individual child psychotherapy, sessions that could be called turning points were analysed.

Method In a series of sessions, five experienced therapists each identified one session that was a ‘turning-point session’ according to the following definition: ‘a session where the therapist notices that something qualitatively new may be identified concerning the behaviour of the child or the child's way of showing his/her inner world, or where something new enters the interplay between the child and the therapist.’

Each therapist was interviewed three times, immediately after the turning-point session, one year later and approximately two years later. Process records, information collected through a questionnaire and the interviews were analysed using a hermeneutic approach.

Results In order to understand the mechanisms behind these therapeutic changes, it is fruitful to study the therapeutic process preceding the turning point, the countertransference of the therapist and changes in the setting of the therapy. The therapists often identified changes when something unpredictable or unusual had happened in the usually rather predictable therapeutic space. Three of the five turning points occurred after interruptions in therapy. Parallel processes in the parents’ therapy and in the therapist's own supervision were other important aspects. A key principle underlying changes of this kind could be described in terms of ‘intersubjectivity’. It is the emotional meeting between two subjects, each influencing the other, which prepares the way for change to take place.

KEYWORDS Child psychotherapy; intersubjectivity; turning points; processes of change; psychodynamics; psychotherapeutic processes.

Deprivation; therapeutic setting; team-work; anti-social tendency; resilience; psychotic reality.

This paper is about the therapeutic process and technique in psychotherapy with deprived children. The need to monitor as a coherent whole both the broader environmental setting and the movements of the transference is illustrated by clinical case material. It is concluded that a) the child's attack on the setting and therapeutic relation has to be picked up and contained both in the transference relationship and in the broader network by the team-work, and b) by carefully following the transference, the child can be helped to a dependent relationship inside which feelings can be made sense of, thus furthering resilience by achieving a better ability to separate good qualities of the self from self-destructive, anti-social aspects of the internal object.

Katherine Arnold  

The title Temperament and Childhood chosen for this collection of papers is reminiscent of the 1950s anthropological studies by Mead and Bateson relating temperament to variables such as culture, sex, and stage of development. However, the perspective of these essays derives more from psychology, though not all the authors are based in that discipline, and the emphasis is more experimental and statistical than observational.

This is a weighty tome, co-authored by forty-three researchers from eleven different countries. It is divided into six sections with a major introductory chapter on each topic which provides an interesting and useful overview. The areas covered are: concepts and measures; temperament and development; temperament and biological processes; application of temperament concepts; cross-cultural, socioeconomic status, sex and other group differences; and, lastly, historical and international perspectives. The book brings together research in progress, recent studies, particularly from the 1980s, and puts it into a perspective which goes back to Hippocrates, who in the fourth century BC introduced the notion of bodily humours, and Galen, who in the second century AD put forward the schema of sanguine, choleric, melancholic and phlegmatic temperaments.

Letter to the Editors from Ms Angela Joyce, Psychoanalyst, London, UK

Angela Joyce

Angela Joyce

25 Drylands Road
London N8 9HN

Angela Joyce  

I wish to comment upon a book review which was published in the April 1997 issue of your journal. In his otherwise interesting review of Joyce McDougall's book ‘The Many Faces of Eros’, David Morgan makes an extraordinary observation, the more so in the context of his earlier comments in the piece. He had been stressing that ‘… it is important for psychoanalytic psychotherapists not to be seduced by the polemic of one organization …’. Then, and one wonders whether it was an act of artistic genius to show the effect on the Subject of a projective identification, he goes on to demonstrate how one can be so seduced.

Commenting on the clinical material in McDougall's book, which apparently shows her as a psychoanalyst, working largely through the technique of reconstruction, he states:

I found this a rather difficult process to follow, no doubt due to my own particular training experience. I am always impressed by how few transference interpretations, if any, occur in the psychoanalysis [sic] by analysts who work from a theoretical basis different from the Kleinian tradition.

This statement is neither substantiated nor elaborated, and so we, the readers, are left wondering what on earth Morgan means by it. Is he suggesting that his training has failed to teach him the variety of techniques used in the psychoanalytic process, which has had the effect of walling him up inside the polemic of one theoretical organization? Is he saying that his, apparently Kleinian, training has led him to write such an extraordinary statement, for which he can have no evidence to substantiate?

Peter Evans

Peter Evans

24 Chequers Road
Basingstoke

Peter Evans  

A 9-year-old girl in weekly treatment recently came to her session very upset that a girl at school had been cruelly making fun of her for being adopted. ‘I wish I'd never told any of the girls at school, now!’ In fact, I think she is re-creating and trying to know about a terrible experience which befell her in her first four, pre-adoptive, years, when she was recurrently molested by her father. The theme she is struggling to deal with is the awful irreversibility of the desanctification of the private, the desecration of the innermost aspects of self. This is the theme which Bollas and Sundelson chronicle in relation to psychoanalysis in this disturbing, urgent and most important book.

Setting their analysis of the loss of psychotherapeutic privacy in the United States of America, the authors provide a sober but deeply alarming account of the legislative and commercial forces which have combined over three decades seriously to undermine the most central aspect of psychoanalysis — the containment afforded by absolute confidentiality. A’ pivotal moment in this saga of third-party interests intruding into the analytic space occurred in 1976, when the parents of a murdered California University student, Sara Tarasoff, successfully sued the Regents of the University for failing to forewarn their daughter of the danger she was facing. She was murdered by another student who had been dating her and who had also been seen in psychotherapy at the Student Health Centre. The California Supreme Court's ruling on this case went down in American legal history, placing an obligation on all therapists to ‘use reasonable care to protect the intended victim’ from the prospect of violence or harm as expressed by any patient in treatment.

Chris Fairhall  

AIDS; prevention; risk-taking; juvenile delinquency; brief group psychotherapy; psychoanalysis.

Brief psychoanalytic groupwork was carried out with two small groups of youths aged 15 to 18 years incarcerated for juvenile offences. The qualitative study of a preventive group intervention for HIV/AIDS risk-taking aims to extend our understanding of, first, the meaning of HIV/AIDS and processes of HIV/AIDS risk-taking in high-risk youths and, second, the mechanisms that may moderate those processes. The specific content of AIDS representations and the intrapersonal developmental processes of human relationships found to underlie the groups’ functioning are more consistent with a psychodynamic model than a ‘rationalist’ model. Three different orientations to AIDS were identified from the intrapersonal and interpersonal patterns and the changes over the course of the sessions demonstrated the value of the groupwork in promoting movement towards greater maturity.

Contentment; smiling; containment; infant observation.

In this paper I examine the importance of the smile as an emotional nexus between infant and mother. A series of observations seems to suggest that the infant is almost immediately able to appreciate when the mother, as a special and separate person, is ready to receive such communication. I consider how a mother's physical and mental embrace may have been altered by the presence of an observer in such a way that the necessary conditions were created for her baby to feel that it was then the right time to use the ability to smile, and so become an active initiator of meaningful interaction.

Letter to the editors from Theodore Mitrani, PhD, California, USA A memorial tribute to Frances Tustin

I am sending you an account of the memorial tribute to Frances Tustin which took place on 21 October 1995 at the Doubletree Hotel in Santa Monica, California and which I hope will be of interest to your readers. Initiated and co-ordinated by Dr Judith Mitrani, the conference was sponsored by the Psychoanalytic Center of California Continuing Education Committee and ably introduced and moderated by PCC President Elect John Lundgren, MD. The audience of over ninety mental health workers was addressed by six speakers, all of whom had a direct connection with Mrs Tustin. The hall where the meeting took place was decorated with poster portraits of Tustin in her youth at the beginning of her career, and up to the month before her death. A video of her BBC interview with Alexander Newman of the Squiggle Foundation was playing continuously at the reception table, where copies of all of her books, generously donated for the occasion by her publishers, Karnac and Routledge, were available for sale to participants.

The first presenter, James Grotstein, MD, attempted to locate Tustin's contribution in the context of contemporary psychoanalytic and psychiatric disciplines. Following a short biographical note, some warm reminiscences about his encounter with Mrs Tustin in Amersham and a number of subsequent phone discussions with her, he proceeded to give a critique of her professional contributions.

Dr Grotstein suggested that Tustin's work was essentially influenced by three psychoanalytic thinkers: Esther Bick and John Bowlby, who were her main instructors in her training years in the Tavistock, and Wilfred Bion, her analyst. Grotstein stated that Tustin's work was an outgrowth of Bick's conceptualization of the ‘second skin’ even though ultimately ‘she was an external objectivist or rehabilitationist, and sided with the object-relations views of Bowlby’. At the same time Grotstein said that it was Bion's theory of thinking which permeated Tustin's work, even though she had openly claimed ‘not to have understood Bion's writings’.

Infant-Led Innovations in a Mother-Baby Therapy Group

Campbell Paul and Frances Thomson-Salo

Frances Thomson-Salo

Parkville, Victoria 3052
Australia

Frances Thomson-Salo  

Mother; infant; group; interaction; attuned play.

A mother-baby therapy group for mothers and infants in their first year who are experiencing difficulties is described. In a literature review no comparable group where the infants are seen as members in their own right has been found. Themes in the mothers’ material are outlined, followed by the infants’ evolving interactive and internal processes. Some therapeutic factors, in particular interactions between the infants and interventions on the part of the therapists, are then illustrated with clinical material. Some infant-led innovations are described, such as the way the infants’ activity is used as a basis for making ‘group as a whole’ interpretations, and in particular how the therapists’ actions towards the infants have come to be viewed as a non-verbal form of interpretation. The role of attuned play in direct work with infants is discussed further.

Facing the Damage Together

Some Reflections Arising from the Treatment in Psychotherapy of a Severely Mentally Handicapped Child

Louise Emanuel

Louise Emanuel

52 Inderwick Rd
London N8

Louise Emanuel  

Mental handicap; self-mutilation; eating disorders; psychoanalytic psychotherapy; attachment.

This paper attempts to explore ideas about the nature of the attachment between a mother and her handicapped or damaged baby. I suggest that when a baby is found to be damaged, at or soon after birth, the parents’ phantasy of a normal ‘beautiful’ baby dies and the mourning process is seldom adequately completed. Unbearable feelings of ‘primary disappointment’ (Emanuel, 1984) experienced by the mother cannot be fully processed, which limits her capacity to provide containment for the infant. The infant may introject a disappointed, hostile or even horrified internal object and may feel herself to be monstrous and worthy only of rejection. The infant's ‘primary handicap’ may be compounded by the development of a ‘secondary handicap’ (Sinason, 1992) — emotional damage — through projective identification with a disappointed, rejecting internal object. I relate these ideas to Donald Meltzer's theory of ‘aesthetic reciprocity’ (1988): his description of the powerful aesthetic impact of the mother and newborn on each other and the effect of noticeable damage in the baby on this aesthetic encounter. These thoughts are illustrated by detailed case material of a 6-year-old severely mentally handicapped girl (brain damaged at birth), who had developed severe ‘secondary handicaps’ — autistic features and eating problems — and who was seen for once weekly psychotherapy. The patient's progress in therapy, as she emerged from a state of autistic withdrawal and autoerotic sexual arousal, is described, and technical and ethical issues arising from the treatment of such a severely damaged child, are discussed.

Dilys Daws  

Feeding problems, weaning, failure to thrive, baby clinic, GP practice,

This paper is based on work in the baby clinic of a general practice, with examples from infant observation, and ideas from recent research. It is something of an interdisciplinary paper.

Feeding and weaning problems are related to issues of closeness and distance between baby and care-giver. In early feeding problems the unmet needs of the parents are crucial. In weaning the use of the spoon as a ‘transitional object’ and as a symbol of the baby's own creative ‘agency’ is described. Later problems may connect with mother's eating disorders, intrusiveness by parents and conflict between parents and baby.

This paper describes the usefulness for the child psychotherapist of some Winnicottian concepts in psychoanalytic treatment of very young psychotic children. Particular attention is given to the concept of ‘potential space’ as Winnicott has formulated it in his writings. Three clinical cases are presented, one of these includes a complete mother-child session in order to show how the therapist can work to create a space where psychic events can become possible.

Liselotte Grünbaum

Liselotte Grünbaum  

Torture-surviving children; massive trauma; repetition compulsion; dissociation; defensive survival strategies; psychotherapy.

Children of refugee families who have survived torture often have emotional, psychosomatic and behavioural problems as well as problems with learning. In order to understand the difficulties of these children, we have to recognize the complicated interaction of cumulative traumatic strain and recurring exposure to shocking violence. The traumatic experiences of the child in the country of origin take place in the broader context of chronic danger and persecution, often to be followed in the country of exile both by recurrent family strain and social estrangement. In the transference this complicated mixture of repeated trauma and chronic strain may show as a pervasive tendency to retreat to defensive survival strategies combined with continual repetition of more specific traces of the impact of the trauma on the individual. This paper focuses on how the enacted survival strategies can be contained and understood in the transference. In due course the compulsive repetition can be given meaning as a precondition for better integration through symbolic thought and self-understanding.

Anne Harrison  

In his review of the history of narcissism as an analytic concept, which forms the initial chapter of this book, David Livingstone Smith makes the observation that psychoanalytic theory does not present itself as a clear and articulated whole, like a Georgian city, but rather as something which has grown organically, over time. In reading through this excellent collection of papers one has the sense of gaining an enormous wealth of insight and understanding, which accumulates, in a similar fashion, organically from one paper to another, but which is never forced into the form of an overarching, general conceptualization.

The concept of narcissism itself is a particularly complex one, having evolved over decades of analytic thinking from a single metapsychological category to include what can be a bewildering range of theories and assumptions, which both characterize and explain a variety of clinical phenomena. The strength of this particular study lies in the directness with which the authors have approached the phenomena of narcissism and have evoked the quality of narcissistic preoccupations and relationships in generous clinical vignettes, and in the sense of authenticity which one feels in each author's struggle to formulate an understanding of his or her experience with patients.

The book is made up of thirteen chapters which are organized in three sections: ‘Overviews’, ‘Narcissism in the Life Cycle’ and ‘Clinical Aspects of Narcissism’. In his chapter on the historical background of the concept, Livingstone Smith provides both a summary of how key figures such as Freud, Klein and Ferenczi conceived of narcissism and a lucid account of the function which this had for each of them in the dynamics of their understanding of the human mind and its motivation. The chapter is particularly useful because it brings into focus from the start the question which runs through the book: how much we may think of the narcissistic insistence of the patients described, and of our own, as having to do with appropriate developmental needs and how much with a malign refusal of relatedness?

David Morgan  

Thank you for allowing me to reply to Angela Joyce's letter. I think she is right to take me to task for what appears to be my criticism of other schools of thought. I have to say that this was not my intention. What I was attempting to convey is how, in an otherwise extremely stimulating and thought provoking book, it was difficult at times for me to feel the clinical examples did justice to the theoretical content. I speculated that in my view this was due to the emphasis on detailed accounts of the patients history and communications to her in the sessions without much illustration of how the analyst actually interacted with this material. I hoped to convey that this could be a lack of understanding on my part, agreeing with Dr McDougall when in her last chapter she writes about the difficulties in talking to each other across the theoretical divides. It was certainly not my intention to be critical of other ways of working, but to reflect on how hard it is sometimes to resonate with very different approaches to interesting clinical phenomena.

Campbell Paul  

This letter was sent to us as a follow-up to the authors’ paper ‘Infant-led innovations in a mother-baby therapy group’ (Journal of Child Psychotherapy, Vol 23, No. 2, August 1997)

We are sending you a summary of our paper on therapeutic work with young infants, which we hope will be of interest to readers. It was presented at the conference titled The Interplay of Infants, Parents and Therapists here in Melbourne in 1996. It represents the work and thinking of the Infant Mental Health Group of the Royal Children's Hospital for more than two decades and marks a departure from currently accepted notions of infant-parent psychotherapy with very young infants.

Our central point was that in doing therapeutic work with infants in the first year we change the infant's internal representations. This has significant effects on interaction and symptoms, and direct work may be particularly indicated where parents seem unable to use their thinking to make links. Clinicians generally hold that if the parents’ representations change there will be a change in interaction and symptom. We are proposing that we examine change in the other direction, if the infant's representations are affected and this impinges on the parents. We made four points: that the infant cannot wait; that if we interact with imitation and attunement it can have a very powerful effect; that experience organizes the brain; and that we may previously have been over-anxious about the parents’ feelings about our involvement.

Peter Evans

24 Chequers Road

Peter Evans  

Trauma, perversion, pathological organization (psychic retreat/labyrinth), hate in the countertransference,

This paper explores the long-term sequelae of chronic early trauma as expressed by an adolescent in intensive psychotherapy. In particular, attention is given to the ways in which intolerable early experience may block subsequent identificatory ego growth by means of a radical defensive detachment from any potential source of help. Healthy maturation is replaced by an elaborate structure of defences aimed at obliterating awareness of unfulfilled attachment needs and providing a constantly available inner sanctum filled with exciting but profoundly unsatisfying sadomasochistic distractions. The technical importance of careful attention to the therapist's countertransference experiences is underlined. It is suggested that the presence of hatred in this area may represent one of the few undistorted communications from the patient, implying hatred of torture and cruelty. As such, when carefully metabolized by the psychotherapist, it may herald the recovery of hope and serve to protect hidden, bullied aspects of the patient's self which are still on the side of life and development.

Edward G. Corrigan and Pearl-Ellen Gordon (eds) The Mind Object: Precocity and Pathology of Self-Sufficiency, London: Karnac, 1995, 245 pp., £19.95.

Eric Rayner

Eric Rayner

43 Heath Hurst Road
London NW3 2RU

Eric Rayner  

This is a memorable book; it is also valuable. Its fourteen contributors come from both sides of the Atlantic — from North America but also Britain. It is an important work for both child and adult analysts and therapists, for, most unusually, they are brought together here under one cover. It is developmental in outlook no matter what age is being addressed. Nearly every chapter has a case study at its axis; the youngest subject is 3, the oldest in his fifties.

As the title indicates, it is about the over-valuation of intellect at the expense of body-feeling. Such over-valuation leads, so the authors argue, to a person experiencing his or her mind as a clever cognitive-functioning ‘thing’ — a marvellous yet self-tormenting agency. This is the ‘mind object’ of the title. We are in the region of narcissistic disorders. Corrigan and Gordon ask: ‘Can a person relate to his mind as an object — depend upon it to the exclusion of other objects — idealize it, fear it, hate it? Can a person live out a life striving to attain the elusive power of his mind's perfection, yielding to its promise while sacrificing the body's truth?’ (p. xiii).

The authors are clear that, though Ferenczi (1933), with his concept of precocious maturity as a response to early trauma, is an inspirational forebear, it is Winnicott who has been seminal. His (1949) paper ‘Mind and its relation to the psyche-soma’ was the first to describe how an individual can respond to very early environmental failure by turning away from body awareness and its needs to establish a conception of intellectual-mental functioning as a ‘thing in itself’. This is the key of the book. Winnicott sees that a violent split allows the mind to negate the role of the body. Such a mental thing in itself can be a substitute for maternal care. It can become an object of intense attachment — giving security and solace. However it can turn on the self and the body — demeaning, accusing and torturing. It is in fact a precocious structuring of the very sense of intellectual development.

Shame in Psychotherapy with Adolescents

Dimitris Anastasopoulos

Dimitris Anastasopoulos

6 Spetson
N. Psychiko
Athens 154 51
Greece

Dimitris Anastasopoulos  

Shame; adolescence; psychotherapy; technique.

Shame has been an insufficiently studied emotion in psychoanalytic literature until recently, mainly because it tended to be ‘absorbed’ under the concept of guilt. Now it is recognized as a powerful affect of pregenital origin, linked with narcissism and the ego ideal. Shame can be a motivation for achievements and social adaptation, it can protect an individual's integrity and can be a modulator of interpersonal relatedness; it can also function as a defence or initiate psychopathological states, such as depression, self-alienation, identity confusion or acting out. In adolescence shame is a ubiquitous phenomenon, as this developmental stage consists of all the parameters that can trigger feelings of shame. The emotional regression connected with the emergence of primitive impulses, conflicts and defences; the grandiose phantasies and the increased narcissism; the preoccupation with bodily functions and body image; the tendency to idealization and the need for social acceptance constitute the matrix within which shame and shame-derived feelings can develop. Shame is discussed as it is experienced by young patients and often by the therapist. Shame in the countertransference and during supervision is also considered. Stress is put on the importance of taking shame into account as a fundamental factor in psychotherapy with adolescents, particularly in relation to the establishment of the therapeutic relationship, understanding and interpretations. The thesis is illustrated with clinical vignettes.

Katherine Arnold

Katherine Arnold

57 Cecile Park
London N8 9AX

Katherine Arnold  

Daniel Stern now has a considerable reputation as a writer and researcher who is able to bring together his own research, and work by different authors from different disciplines, notably developmental psychology

310

and psychoanalysis. This book is an academic book, in contrast to some of his recent work written for a lay audience, and covers a broad spectrum of ideas. He is interested in psychotherapy in general, and in work with mothers and infants in particular. He has been able to draw together workers in the field, who have diverse perspectives and views, to undertake original research together. But one of the frustrations of the book, for this reader at least, was the lack of detail of the work done together, which sounds as if it must have been fascinating. Generally there is a lack of clinical detail through the book. It was not possible for me to get a picture of Stern at work, although there were many ideas to consider and explore.

The motherhood constellation is defined as the new and unique psychic organization a woman enters into at the birth of a baby, of unspecified duration, months or years. John Byng-Hall has suggested extending the concept into a consideration of parenthood constellation. Stern mentions fathers rather briefly, and links their role very concretely to the child care they take on. Stern argues that the motherhood constellation is a state of mind which takes over from the usual preoccupations and concerns of the mother. He contrasts it with the Oedipal complex, and writes about the implications of terms such as ‘complex’. He wishes to use the term constellation to avoid the implications of psycho-pathology, which he feels are implied by the notion of a complex. As always with such examination of concepts, there are many assumptions behind the words used.

Stern uses concepts developed in his earlier works, notably The Interpersonal World of the Infant (1985), but he has developed and refined his ideas. He now writes of ‘schemas-of-being-with’ which are intended to provide ways of investigating and thinking about the ordinary everyday experiences of the individual, something like the atmosphere of a family or an interaction. To elicit these schemas he advocates the use of a technique he calls the micro-analytic interview. The aim, as in earlier work by Stern, is to elaborate upon the representations an individual has built up from past experience. To do this he suggests concentrating upon an emergent moment. The moment he chooses is breakfast on an ordinary day. The idea is to consider in detail a time deliberately chosen to be as free as possible of ‘psychodynamically important moments’. Interviewees are asked to elaborate their thoughts around this in many ways, including to imagine filming the moment. They are not asked to make links to past experience, but Stern tells us that they nearly always do take up this perspective. Using this information Stern deduces various ‘schemas-of-being-with’ important to that individual.

Silence and Survival: Working with Strategies of Denial in Families of Traumatized Pre-School Children

Kjerstin Almqvist and Anders Broberg

Anders Broberg

Box 9104
S-65009, Karlstad
Sweden

Anders Broberg  

Post-traumatic symptoms; re-enacting play; family dynamics; refugees.

Silence and denial about previous traumatic experiences are common features in families exposed to organized violence. Mutual protection between family members, and especially between parents and children, is seen as the fundament for the silencing of traumatic experiences. This strategy is suggested to have adaptive advantages in dangerous situations in general, where it serves the function of saving the child's internal representations of his/her parents as secure bases. If, however, the dangerous situation escalates and a psychic trauma cannot be avoided, the strategy of mutual silence concerning the event(s) becomes an obstacle for giving traumatized children parental support and professional treatment. It is argued that clinicians need to take seriously the strong reasons families have for upholding their strategy of denial, if they want to help traumatized families to a better functioning. A case presentation is made to illustrate how it is possible to use refugee children's re-enacting play as a source of information about past traumatic events in order to change destructive post-traumatic family dynamics and improve parental support to the child.
